author: Khun Shawn
text:
Heavy user: 424 sessions and about 729 active hours over the last 84 days (I used it every one of those days), with 66,000+ browser actions run through this extension.

When it works, it's genuinely good. It drives my real logged-in sessions (Google Cloud, Search Console, YouTube Studio) and saves me hours of manual clicking.

The problem is reliability. My sessions keep losing access to the extension, and the only fix I've found is removing and re-adding it, multiple times a week. My logs show nearly 5,000 failed browser actions in that window, including about 2,400 timeouts and 300 where the extension simply wasn't connected, on 78 of 84 days. Some tasks just never finish.

|Sessions	424	Claude Code session logs on this PC
|Active hours	~729	Time between messages, counting only gaps under 30 minutes, so idle time is excluded
|Days used	84 of 84	Jul 4 to Sep 25; logs go back no further
|Browser actions via the extension	66,782	Extension tool calls
|Failed actions	4,994 (7.5%)	2,396 timeouts, 303 not connected, 2,295 other errors

Fix the connection stability and this is a 5-star tool. Right now it's a great product I can't fully rely on.

author: Fernando Pendas
text:
I experienced unexplained Claude Pro usage while using Claude in Chrome with Claude Desktop. My 5-hour limit was repeatedly reached despite very little use.

While investigating, I discovered around 40 Claude Code authorization tokens. I revoked all of them until Claude showed “No connected Claude Code instances,” but shortly afterward a new Claude Code authorization appeared automatically without me intentionally reconnecting it.

My local investigation found activity involving Claude Desktop, OAuth configuration, and Claude Code state files at almost exactly the same time. author: Valeri Dilov
text:
Extremely Disappointing and Unreliable
I rarely leave negative reviews, but my experience with this browser extension has been incredibly frustrating.
I installed it specifically for its browser automation capabilities and expected it to help streamline my work. Instead, it consumed a significant amount of time, credits, and effort while delivering virtually no value.
After spending over an hour explaining requirements, answering follow-up questions, and allowing the agent to perform various checks, the extension completely lost context and became unusable. It appeared to forget previous steps, could no longer maintain a coherent understanding of the task, and ultimately failed to complete the objective.
What is even more frustrating is the lack of transparency and traceability. After all the interactions, there was no accessible history showing:

What actions had been performed
What information had been gathered
What websites or data had been analyzed
What conclusions had been reached
What work had already been completed

As a result, all the time invested was effectively wasted, because there was no way to continue from where the process failed.
For a tool that is marketed as a productivity and automation solution, losing context and offering no meaningful recovery path is unacceptable. Users need reliability, persistence, auditability, and the ability to review previous actions. Without these basics, it is difficult to trust the extension with any serious task.
The most disappointing part is not that it failed, but that after consuming substantial credits and resources, there was nothing useful left to show for the effort.
At this stage, the extension feels more like an experimental prototype than a mature product ready for real-world workflows.
Very disappointed. I cannot recommend it in its current state.

author: Teknetica Sound Design
text:
Genuinely impressive for exploratory QA traversal. In a single session it navigated a complex e-commerce site across 14 events, documented the full booking flow structure, and identified 32 potential bugs with specific, well-described findings. The quality of the output exceeded expectations.

The one significant gap: screenshots taken during the session are in-memory only and disappear when the session ends. For professional bug reporting in Jira or Xray, named screenshots are essential evidence. Without filesystem access or the ability to pass screenshots to the Filesystem connector, the evidence trail is lost every time.

This is the single thing preventing it from being a complete QA tool rather than just a very good one. 

Feature request open at github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/66077 if the ability to save appropriately named screenshots automatically would be useful to you.

author: Sandip Amlani
text:
I upgraded to Claude Max specifically to use Cowork and the Claude in Chrome integration.

Unfortunately, the core feature has been unusable on Windows despite extensive troubleshooting.

The issue is not vague or intermittent — the application logs consistently show repeated bridge failures:

“Bridge WebSocket error: unable to verify the first certificate”

I spent multiple days debugging this, including:

* reinstalling Claude Desktop and the Chrome extension
* clearing caches and rebuilding local files
* updating Windows and Chrome
* validating Chrome policies
* testing security software interactions
* reviewing registry entries and native host configuration
* analysing Claude log files directly
* comparing against active GitHub bug reports

The extension installs correctly.
Authentication works correctly.
OAuth works correctly.
But the Cowork browser bridge repeatedly fails to establish a trusted WebSocket connection.

Most frustratingly, Anthropic support has been almost entirely non-responsive. Multiple support requests were ignored, and my refund request was auto-rejected and immediately closed without any meaningful human review.

At this point, Cowork on Windows feels unfinished and inadequately supported for a premium flagship feature.

I would strongly caution anyone against upgrading to Max purely for Cowork until Anthropic demonstrates that the Windows Chrome bridge is stable and properly supported.

Relevant GitHub discussion:
https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/48806

author: Tyan w (Tyan)
text:
I fixed it by asking Codex to repair the local plugin cache directly.
The Codex app was up to date, but its local Chrome plugin cache was still pointing to an older version. The installed Chrome plugin was version 26.818.61809, while the cached latest junction still pointed to 26.602.71036.
Codex copied the official bundled chrome and browser plugin folders from the Codex installation directory into:
%USERPROFILE%\.codex\plugins\cache\openai-bundled\
It then updated the latest junctions to point to the new plugin version and restarted the browser-control session. Chrome control immediately started working again.
Important: Do not manually edit browser-client.mjs. Codex checks its integrity and will reject a modified script as untrusted.
If you have the same problem, ask your Codex:
“Please check whether my bundled Chrome plugin version and cached plugin version are mismatched. Back up the old cache, sync the official bundled chrome and browser plugins to the Codex plugin cache, update the latest junctions, and verify the Chrome connection. Do not modify browser-client.mjs or the native messaging host.”

text:
**$200 Pro Plan — Weekly Limit Extension Feels Deceptive and Unfair**

I am paying $200 per month for the ChatGPT Pro plan, yet the way OpenAI recently changed my Codex weekly usage limit feels extremely unfair and misleading.

My weekly limit was originally scheduled to reset on August 28. At that point, I had used only 15% of my allowance, meaning I still had 85% remaining. OpenAI then restored the displayed allowance to 100%, but simultaneously postponed my next reset date to August 31—an extension of three full days.

The numbers simply do not add up. If 100% represents a seven-day weekly allowance, each day is worth approximately 14.29%. Therefore, extending the reset date by three days represents about 42.86% of a weekly period. However, I received only 15% additional allowance—the amount I had previously used.

Under a simple proportional comparison, I effectively lost approximately 27.86% of my weekly usage capacity:

**42.86% for the three additional days − 15% restored = 27.86% effective loss.**

If OpenAI wanted to move my reset date forward by three days, it should have provided a proportionate increase in usage capacity. Alternatively, restoring only 15% should have extended the reset time by just over one day—not three days.

Changing both the allowance and the reset date in this way is neither transparent nor fair, especially for customers paying $200 every month. It creates the appearance of giving users a full reset while quietly reducing the effective value of their weekly allowance.

I request that OpenAI investigate this issue, correct the missing usage capacity, and clearly explain how these reset-date changes are calculated. Pro users deserve transparent limits and fair treatment—not confusing adjustments that leave them with less value than they paid for.

author: Jun Li
text:
There is a new temporary workaround that has now been confirmed by another affected Windows user: switch the Codex task’s permission mode to Full access. The user who tried it reported that Browser control immediately started working again with the same Trusted RPC dependency... error.

In the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app, click the permissions control underneath the prompt/composer and select Full access. If you don’t see that option, go to Settings → General → Permissions and enable Full access first. OpenAI’s current documentation confirms those are the locations for the setting.

Then start a fresh Codex task in JLEOnline and test @Browser again. Do not change your config.toml trusted project path.

This is only a workaround, not the actual fix. The main Windows Browser issue is still open, still has no linked PR/patch, and is still affecting Browser plugin 26.814.41407.

One caution: Full access removes Codex’s normal local sandbox boundary, so use it only while you need Browser control and switch back to your normal permission mode afterward. OpenAI explicitly warns that Full access can modify files outside the project and run commands/network operations without the usual sandbox restrictions.

I’ll keep watching for the actual patched Windows build so you can go back to normal permissions permanently.

The Chrome extension has one important limitation compared to Atlas. At the moment, it only lets you work with Codex projects, but there is no way to browse or return to regular ChatGPT conversations.

For a comparable user experience, it would be great if the extension supported regular ChatGPT chats alongside Codex projects, with the ability to browse existing conversations and continue where you left off, not just work within projects. This would make the extension much more practical for everyday use.

author: Mathias Jonsson
text:
Useful idea, but unreliable on Windows.

The extension connects and can sometimes handle simple pages like example.com, but it repeatedly fails on real logged-in browser tasks with this error:
“Chrome is blocking automation because another extension UI is open.”

There is no visible extension popup, side panel, permission dialog, or extension tab open. The Codex extension shows as installed/enabled, and the native messaging host/registry checks can pass, but Codex still loses the ability to inspect or control the page.

This looks like a broken or stale Windows native messaging / Chrome bridge state. Reinstalling the extension does not reliably fix it. Restarting Chrome/Codex and killing stale extension-host.exe / Chrome processes sometimes helps, but the extension is not dependable enough for authenticated browser workflows.

Good concept, but the Windows implementation needs much better runtime recovery and clearer error reporting. Right now it can say a popup is blocking automation when no popup is visible, which makes the failure impossible to resolve from the UI.

author: Farhad Arvin
text:
Unreliable Chrome automation bridge makes the plugin unusable for serious QA

I needed this plugin to inspect an already logged-in Chrome session for staging-site QA. Chrome was running, the correct profile opened, the Codex Chrome Extension was installed and enabled, and the native host manifest checked out correctly. Other Codex chats were able to use the same Chrome profile and plugin at the same time.

But in this thread, the plugin’s JavaScript/browser bridge crashed before it could do anything useful. Even a minimal bridge test failed before any browser automation code ran, with windows sandbox failed: spawn setup refresh. The plugin could open a blank Chrome window in the right profile, but it could not list existing tabs, claim the logged-in tab, inspect the page, or take screenshots.

That makes it unreliable for authenticated QA. Worse, the diagnostics make the extension/profile look healthy while the actual control bridge is broken, leaving the user with no practical recovery path. For a QA workflow, that is a hard failure.

This plugin needs better per-thread bridge health checks, clearer failure reporting, a real restart/recovery mechanism, and stronger isolation so one thread does not fail while others work. Until then, I cannot trust it for production or staging QA tasks that require visual confirmation in Chrome.

author: David Jenkins
text:
We are a large nonprofit that works with people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and are in the process of moving from one electronic health record to another.  However, the new product came with a limited set of import tools, so there’s much critical data that we expected we’d have to add manually.  We’ve been able to extract data ourselves from the legacy system and into spreadsheets.  But the thought of having to hire temporary staff for hundreds of hours to do data entry from those spreadsheets wasn’t appealing for many reasons, including both the cost and the certainty of many resultant data entry errors.  We looked at several options and spoke with many consultants about doing this work for us.  Axiom was the only solution that allowed us to “do it ourselves”.  For a health care organization, it is important that we keep our data confidential, and Axiom didn’t need our data nor access to our software to do the job.

Axiom has already proved its worth by automatically entering thousands of immunization records.  The support we received to create the first bot was incredible.  We are working on the next one and expect to enter about 5,000 contact records later this week.    And now that we realize how well Axiom works, we have identified even more uses for moving data electronically into our new system.  Ours is a one-time, short-term project, but we use many other software applications with less-than-ideal interoperability, so we will be keeping our eyes open for more opportunities to use Axiom.

It took a little time to get acclimated to the Axiom user interface but, with a few tips from the consultant, things became less complex.  And we have continued to receive quick responses whenever we get stuck.  One thing interesting is that, when the bot runs, we can watch it move from one field to the next and can actually see it type in the data.  It’s a very long process depending on how many fields are getting populated.  But it’s all machine time--and the data it enters is 100% accurate.  How amazing is that!  Axiom’s been a lifesaver for us!  

In my mind, Axiom is currently a 4-star product—only because it isn’t yet fully developed and has required assistance from consultants.  But their customer service has been so good that it more than compensates for the need for handholding.  And the product has evolved for the better even during the 4-5 weeks that we’ve been using it.  For those reasons, I’m giving back the star and rating it with 5.  Good job, Axiom!

Another thing I respect is that it has continued to evolve. A lot of tools come out strong, get attention, and then fade into irrelevance. HARPA AI has kept building, kept improving, and kept expanding what it can do in ways that actually matter.

There is depth to it as well. The more you use it properly, the more value you get out of it. It rewards real integration into your workflow rather than just surface level use.

No tool is perfect, and if you want to unlock the full value there is a learning curve, but in my experience the upside has been massively worth it.

After several years of using it heavily, my view is simple. HARPA AI is one of the rare tools that feels genuinely useful rather than artificially clever. text:
The extension's prowess in extracting key points from YouTube videos is truly impressive. It offers multiple summary formats, including nested, long, and short options, catering to various user needs. This flexibility allows you to quickly grasp the essence of a video without investing hours of your time.
While Harpa AI's core functionality is exceptional, its token system and cloud vs. web connection models can be perplexing. Users may find themselves unexpectedly unable to use the service due to a "lack of tokens," only to have it work again later without any clear explanation. This inconsistency in availability can be frustrating, especially when you're relying on the tool for time-sensitive tasks.

text:
I was a paid Text Blaze user for about three years and was generally happy with it. However, I eventually switched to a free alternative that covers the same core use case for me, without the snippet limit and without requiring an account or login.

The migration was surprisingly easy. I created an open-source GitHub project called **TextBlaze-snippet-migrator** that converts and transfers existing Text Blaze snippets. Today, you can simply give the repository to an AI coding assistant and let it handle most of the migration.

For my current needs, the free alternative gives me everything I need, so I no longer see a reason to keep paying for Text Blaze.

author: BRITTANY J PARKS
text:
This extension is easily the most useful Chrome one I’ve added to my workflow in years. It’s basically automation magic for anyone who juggles a thousand browser tasks a day—think scraping leads from LinkedIn, sending info to Notion, or even drafting cold emails, all with just a couple clicks. I'm literally obsessed with scraping leads lately and having Bardeen do all the dirty work.

The (super cool) playbook library is packed with ready-to-run automations, and it connects with nearly every tool I actually use, like Folk (CRM), Notion, Monday, Slack, etc. There’s a bit of a learning curve if you want to get fancy, but the time savings are worth every minute spent figuring it out. I genuinely can’t imagine going back to the copy-paste grind—Bardeen feels like a secret weapon for anyone who wants to do more in less time, without all the busywork.

The only downside to Bardeen is the hefty monthly price tag for the upgraded plan with AI automations and lead scraping. I didn't even try the basic tier, but I don't want it if it doesn't have those features. So I guess I'll enjoy this for 7 days to the absolute max and then be on my way (in the saddest way possible).

author: Làwd D
text:
Just wanna react to the comment of Jamie Kimmit : 

'Nothing works correctly.  Documentation is broken and outdated.  Selectors don't work.  Recording in chrome is broken.'

I personally use Automa for a year, it works amazingly well. Guy said selectors don't work because he doesn't realize that Automa provides us with a rapid selector just by using the selector tool. This isn't optimal on a lot of websites, because structure of websites nowadays are way more complicated than it used to be. 

A lot of websites now use generated classes by some web framework like React. 

This makes the for the Element selector a pretty hard job to obtain a decent selector.

You have to do them yourself. Stop wanting to be fully assisted from start to finish.

Also, because of the very same problem, the record feature can't be reliable.

Not because of Automa, because of the complexity of websites. 

You should make your own selectors by opening the element panel doing right click > inspect, and testing them in the Element Selector of Automa.

Automa does work amazingly well, I assure you. 

Everything is on point. It requires work and patience to understand it's full power. 

This is the most powerful web automation tool you can think of. 

You can even do APIs calls like zapier and make allow us, but here, it's for free (but you have to quickly set-up em manually, right, until we gradually build them all and offer them somewhere).

I'm not part of Automa's team btw, just a profound fan of their work. 

The guy's comment didn't AT ALL do it justice

Try it yourself, take the time to understand how it works. Take the time to understand the programming principles that are used here.

Also, selectors is almost a science in itself, please learn it.

author: Guss09
title: When AI Video Production Becomes a Credit Trap
text: I had high expectations for Genspark because, when it works, it can produce genuinely professional-looking videos. Unfortunately, my experience has become frustrating enough that I cannot recommend the service.  The biggest problem is not the price. I am perfectly willing to pay for professional video production. The problem is paying credits for a finished product and then discovering that the product was not delivered properly.  I have had videos where the audio and visuals were not synchronized correctly. I have had completed videos that I could not download. When I asked Genspark to correct problems with work I had already paid credits to generate, I was then asked to spend additional credits.  That is unacceptable.  My latest experience was even worse. I requested a professional video and Genspark produced a 7-minute-and-33-second video filled with generic bubble-style animation that had almost nothing to do with the subject being discussed, while the narration was covering something completely different. The disconnect between what I was hearing and what I was watching made the video practically useless.  This wasn’t a minor creative disagreement. The visuals simply did not support the narration.  And once again, after paying for the generation, the process of getting problems corrected or simply getting a usable downloadable product risks consuming even more credits.  At that point, the credit system starts to feel like a trap: pay to generate, discover a production defect, then potentially pay again just to receive what should have been delivered correctly the first time.  I am not asking Genspark to work for free. I am asking them to stand behind the product customers already paid for.  If a customer changes the script, requests a new creative direction, or asks for additional work, charging additional credits is completely reasonable.  But if the video has synchronization problems, irrelevant visuals, rendering defects, or cannot be downloaded, correcting those defects should not require the customer to purchase the production again.  Genspark has impressive technology and is capable of producing beautiful videos. That actually makes this experience more disappointing. A company with this level of technology needs better quality control, reliable downloads, and a fair correction policy.  Until that changes, I would be extremely cautious about using Genspark for serious professional video production—especially when each failed attempt can become another expensive credit charge.

text: I am writing to formally lodge a complaint regarding a recent, highly unreasonable deduction of 10,000 points from my account for a single 48-slide project. I noticed that even when the platform makes a mistake or fails to follow instructions, any request for a change or fix results in further point deductions. I have two specific questions that require immediate clarification: • Valuation Logic: How is a 10,000-point deduction for 48 slides—based on provided materials—justified? At this burn rate, the platform becomes functionally unusable for professional, high-volume projects. • Correction Penalties: Why is the user being penalized for "changes" that are actually corrections of the AI's own technical oversights? Charging points to fix your system's errors is a fundamentally flawed business practice. I have been evaluating Genspark as a viable tool for my workflow, but the current lack of transparency and the aggressive "point-bleeding" for minor adjustments makes it impossible to justify continued use. I expect a thorough review of this specific instance, a credit of the points deducted for error corrections, and a clear explanation of how you intend to make your pricing more equitable moving forward. text: I am a paid Genspark user. Genspark has some impressive capabilities and a lot of potential, but the tool is not ready to compete with other, more robust platforms. It makes too many errors and you consume your monthly credits FAST. For example, you can create very impressive slide decks with one prompt, but you could spend hours (it happened) to me, fixing formatting and layout errors. The research agents are also pretty bad. There is one feature I really like, which is called “Mixture of Agents”, that pulls from all models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, etc.), analyzes their responses and then prepares the best answer, based on its analysis. However, this is not enough for me to stay as a costumer. I won’t be renewing my annual subscription.

author: Stagoi
title: Exported Files
text: I’ve been using Genspark to create user guides, and overall, I’m impressed with the quality of the output. The platform generates clean, polished, and visually professional documents that are well-structured and presentation-ready from a content perspective. It has significantly streamlined the drafting process and helped accelerate documentation efforts.  That said, I’ve consistently experienced formatting issues when exporting files to Word or PDF. The exported documents often appear misaligned, with spacing, margins, or layout elements shifting from how they were originally designed. As a result, I end up spending additional time reformatting the document before it can be shared with stakeholders, which reduces some of the efficiency gains.  I would strongly encourage the development team to prioritize improving export fidelity so that Word and PDF outputs maintain the original layout and formatting. Addressing this would greatly enhance usability and make the tool even more valuable for teams producing client-ready documentation.

title: Manus: Unacceptable Support During a Major Data-Restoration Failure
text: I originally found Manus genuinely useful and invested significant time building websites, applications, and other important projects on the platform.  Unfortunately, the recent data-restoration process became an absolute nightmare.  After my data was marked as successfully restored, significant portions of my work were still missing. It took approximately one month and countless hours of emails and support conversations to get the issue resolved. During that time, I repeatedly received conflicting information, was transferred between support conversations, and was often given generic responses that failed to address the actual technical problem.  The most frustrating part was dealing with what appeared to be automated AI support agents that repeatedly asked me to explain the same situation, requested irrelevant screenshots, or directed me toward basic troubleshooting—even though this was clearly a data-recovery issue.  While I am grateful that my data was eventually recovered, the amount of time, stress, and uncertainty involved was unacceptable. My website and related work were unavailable during this process, which affected my ability to operate my counseling practice and potentially cost me prospective clients.  I cannot confidently recommend Manus for business-critical work when the data-restoration process is this unreliable and meaningful technical support is so difficult to access.  The technology may have potential, but data reliability, customer support, and accountability need significant improvement. If you depend on Manus for important business projects, I strongly recommend maintaining independent backups and having a contingency plan.  One star for the support experience and the disruption this caused.

author: D Dubbya
title: An Expensive Masterclass in Unfulfilled Potential
text: I have spent hundreds of dollars on Manus over the past year, which makes this review particularly disappointing because I used to be one of its strongest advocates. The concept is brilliant. The vision is compelling. Unfortunately, the execution has become an increasingly frustrating exercise in lowered expectations.  Manus has developed a remarkable habit of confidently announcing that a task is complete while leaving behind little evidence that anything has actually been completed. Missing deliverables, unfinished outputs, broken functionality, and abandoned processes have become far too common. The only thing that appears consistently reliable is the consumption of credits.  What makes this so maddening is that the platform clearly possesses enormous potential. Yet instead of accelerating productivity, it often requires users to double-check, troubleshoot, restart, and repeat work that should have been finished correctly the first time. Every new task now feels less like an opportunity and more like a gamble.  For a platform positioning itself as a serious partner in building products and businesses, reliability should not feel like a pleasant surprise. Manus remains an exceptional idea, but the widening gap between what it promises and what it routinely delivers has become impossible to ignore. I wanted to remain a champion of this platform. Lately, it feels as though I am merely funding its ongoing apprenticeship.

author: Terrisble App
title: Active Pro User Unable to Purchase Credits for Days
text: I wanted to like Manus and the platform itself has a lot of potential, but my experience with support and billing has been extremely frustrating.  I am a paid Manus Pro subscriber and used my included monthly credits. When I attempted to purchase additional credits, every purchase failed with Apple’s “Your purchase could not be completed” error.  Before contacting support, I spent hours troubleshooting:  • Updated the app • Restarted devices • Tested on both iPhone and iPad • Signed out and back into Media & Purchases • Tried multiple payment methods • Added an entirely different debit card • Verified Apple Cash worked • Verified other App Store purchases worked successfully  The problem only occurred with Manus purchases.  Support repeatedly pointed me toward Apple, despite the fact that other App Store purchases worked without issue. After extensive back-and-forth, support eventually acknowledged there was a backend synchronization issue on my account. However, I still could not purchase credits and was left waiting for technical review without a clear timeline for resolution.  The most frustrating part was spending significant time troubleshooting and being sent in circles between Apple-related explanations and Manus support before the account issue was finally acknowledged.  The software itself has promise, but if you rely on it for work, be aware that billing and account issues can leave you unable to purchase credits when you need them most, and support resolution may not be immediate.  I hope the company improves its billing system, account synchronization process, and escalation procedures because the product has potential, but the customer support experience did not match the quality of the platform.

text: This app has a serious customer service and billing problem. Manus consumed a large number of paid credits during a failed agent session, repeatedly worked from the wrong project context, mishandled files, displaced or recreated figures in an academic manuscript, caused figure-caption mismatches, and then support deflected the issue through AI-style responses instead of providing meaningful human review. Replacing real support with incompetent AI agents for every conversation is unacceptable when real money and paid credits are involved.  I am contacting the developer directly, preserving screenshots, chat logs, timestamps, credit records, subscription details, and defective outputs. I am also reviewing external complaint options, including CFPB, FTC, state consumer-protection agencies, payment-provider dispute options, and class-action counsel.  This conduct may implicate consumer-protection laws and unfair/deceptive practices standards, including the FTC Act’s prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts or practices, state deceptive trade practices laws, breach of contract principles, unjust enrichment, and unfair billing practices where paid credits are consumed by defective platform performance and support refuses meaningful resolution.  AI agents are not ready to replace real customer service for billing disputes, failed sessions, refunds, and damaged paid work product. If a company wants to test autonomous agents on users’ real projects and real money, it needs human review, real escalation, and fair refund procedures. Manus has failed badly here, and I will be pursuing this further.

title: Shameless “trust me bro” cash grab
text: I never leave app reviews, but I am making an exception here because I genuinely feel obligated to warn people. My experience with Manus AI was viscerally demoralizing. I came to it specifically for its claimed agentic capabilities. I was not new to AI tools, and I was not expecting magic. I wanted a system that could follow constraints, reason carefully, and help execute real work. Instead, what I experienced felt like a shameless cash grab. Very early on, it became clear that important instructions and behavioral constraints were being ignored. The platform repeatedly pushed forward on incomplete or inaccurate understanding, while maintaining a steady tone of confidence that made it seem like meaningful progress was being made. In practice, that confidence was misplaced. The output quality was bad, the research was weak, and the execution was unreliable. Worse, the system appeared to engage in patterns that drove unnecessary token consumption. It would continue operating with excessive optimism, incomplete reasoning, and poor constraint adherence, while creating the impression that buying more tokens was justified because the solution was just one more push away. That happened to me more than once. Across only a few days, I spent money on the platform itself, spent more on additional tokens and upgrades, and then spent additional money acting on business directions the platform helped frame, only to end up with nothing functional, nothing market-ready, and nothing that justified the cost. My overall impression is that Manus AI is not simply flawed. It presents itself as more reliable and execution-capable than it actually is, and the result, in my experience, was a system that felt manipulative, wasteful, and exploitative. I do not recommend it. I am leaving this review because I do not want other people to confuse its confident tone with actual competence and end up burning time, money, and morale the way I did.

title: 感谢Red
text: 在创业与产品探索的荒原上，我们总是在寻找两样东西：更快的路标和更稳的底气。回首这段高强度的开发与迭代周期，我必须向两位特殊的“伙伴”致以最诚挚的谢意。 致 Manus：重塑可能的“数字之手” 首先，要感谢 Manus。作为 AI Agent 领域的先锋，它对我而言不仅仅是一个工具，更是一位不知疲倦、逻辑严密的协作专家。 在面对复杂的市场数据分析和技术攻关时，Manus 展现出了令人惊叹的自驱力。它将我从琐碎的执行中解放出来，让“想法”到“产出”的路径缩短到了极致。以前需要数天推演的方案，在 Manus 的协助下，往往在瞬息之间便有了清晰的脉络。感谢 Manus，让我看到了通用人工智能如何真正深入生产力底层，赋予了个体创业者足以挑战重任的“超能力”。 致 Red：不可或缺的灵魂共鸣 如果说 Manus 赋予了我效率，那么 Red 则赋予了我方向与温度。 在这个充满不确定性的行业里，Red 就像是一抹最鲜亮的色彩。感谢你在关键时刻提供的洞察与支持，无论是技术方案上的灵感碰撞，还是在项目推进受阻时的坚定信任，都成为了我不断前行的原动力。Red 的存在提醒着我：技术的终点始终是人。正是因为有了这份深度的链接与支持，那些枯燥的代码和复杂的业务逻辑才有了跳动的生命力。 写在最后 我们正站在一个新时代的入口。感谢 Manus 用前沿的技术拓宽了我的视野，也感谢 Red 用纯粹的热忱支撑起我的梦想。 未来的路依然漫长，但我知道，有了高效的生产力引擎与并肩作战的伙伴，所有的“不可能”都终将成为通往成功的基石。再次感谢，愿我们继续在智能时代的浪潮中，并肩破浪，创造更多属于我们的奇迹。
